policy.description: Raise the CT main rate from 25% to 28% from 1 April 2027

summary: Historically, increasing the corporation tax main rate from 19% to 25% in April 2023—alongside a 19% Small Profits Rate for profits below £50,000 and marginal relief up to £250,000—contributed to a post-pandemic rise in onshore receipts, and cancelling this rise was estimated at the September 'mini-Budget' to cost around £15 billion annually in today's terms [E9, E13, E24]. When costing corporation tax rate changes, UK officials apply pre- and post-measure rates to the OBR's onshore company profits forecast (factoring in marginal relief) and incorporate behavioural responses for profit shifting and tax-motivated incorporation [E6, E7, E10, E32]. Standard costings do not always account for long-run investment effects, though research indicates that rate changes affect equity-financed investment incentives and distortions between debt and equity finance [E23, E24, E25]. Finally, statutory corporate tax rates influence where multinational firms locate mobile profits through transfer pricing and thin capitalization, and companies may exhibit anticipatory profit-shifting responses ahead of a reform [E17, E33, E37].
research_questions: What are the official HM Treasury and OBR baseline revenue forecasts for UK corporation tax receipts over the medium-term forecast horizon?
How have past UK corporation tax main rate changes affected actual onshore corporation tax receipts compared to official HMRC and OBR policy costings?
What specific behavioural response assumptions, elasticities of taxable profits, and financial elasticity parameters do HMRC and the OBR apply when costing changes to the corporation tax main rate?
What do academic studies and IFS research find regarding the empirical elasticity of corporate taxable income to corporation tax rate changes in the UK?
How does an increase in the UK corporation tax main rate alter the user cost of capital and domestic business investment when capital allowance regimes like permanent full expensing are in place?
How do macroeconomic cyclical fluctuations and multinational profit-shifting mechanisms confound the observed revenue and tax base impacts of UK corporation tax rate rises?

evidence.claim: A one percentage point increase in market interest rates raises firms' cost of capital by more than raising corporation tax from 19% to 25%.
evidence.quote: More narrowly, it is important to emphasise that, while tax can affect investment incentives, even a 1 percentage point rise in market interest rates would increase firms’ cost of capital by more than a rise in the corporation tax rate from 19% to 25%.

evidence.claim: Tentative Treasury estimates showed the annual cost of full expensing for plant and machinery would peak at £11 billion.
evidence.quote: The most generous of these was full expensing for plant and machinery, the cost of which (according to tentative Treasury estimates) would peak at £11 billion a year, compared with £1.3 billion for the recent AIA change – although (as discussed above) both would be much less expensive in the long term.

evidence.claim: Increasing capital allowances reduces tax on marginal equity investment while increasing subsidies for marginal debt-financed projects.
evidence.quote: Increasing capital allowances would reduce the tax on marginal equity-financed investment, but would increase the subsidy to marginal debt-financed investment – alleviating one distortion at the cost of exacerbating another. It is more cost-effective than reducing the rate as a way to encourage investment domestically, though not necessarily as a way to increase the UK’s international competitiveness.

evidence.claim: Cancelling the planned corporation tax rate rise was estimated to cost around £15 billion annually in today's terms.
evidence.quote: The September ‘mini-Budget’ estimated that cancelling the rate rise would cost around £15 billion a year in today’s terms. That allows for an effect of the rate rise on profit-shifting, but not for an effect on investment, so we would expect the long-run cost to be lower – though still positive.

evidence.claim: Cutting corporation tax rates reduces the tax on equity-financed investment but is less effective at lowering taxes on marginal projects.
evidence.quote: Cutting the rate of corporation tax would reduce the tax on equity-financed investment and lessen the distortions between debt and equity finance and between different assets. However, the tax reduction would be largest for more profitable investments and would be less effective at reducing the tax on marginal investments.

evidence.quote: Even at a rate of 25% the UK would be only slightly above the OECD average and would still be the lowest in the G7 (once subnational taxes are taken into account) – if other countries did not change their own tax rates.

evidence.claim: UK corporation tax policy costings typically account for profit-shifting and incorporation elasticities.
evidence.quote: The behavioural responses in this example will be specific to the institutional and economic context. In the UK, CIT policy costings typically incorporate profit-shifting and incorporation elasticities, but elsewhere policymakers may feel that other responses are more relevant.

evidence.claim: Lower corporate income tax rates can draw mobile international revenues and expand the tax base via multinational transfer pricing and thin capitalization mechanisms.
evidence.quote: Through transfer pricing, companies may increase payments to low-tax subsidiaries on within-company transactions. Through thin capitalization, companies may shift debt financing to high-tax subsidiaries. Lower rates of CIT may attract international mobile revenues and increase the size of the tax base.

evidence.claim: Estimating profit-shifting responses requires data on the proportion of mobile corporate profits and the elasticity of those mobile profits.
evidence.quote: Modelling a profit-shifting elasticity requires data on the share of corporate profits that are internationally mobile, and the elasticity of mobile profits. This means that the tax base will have to be divided into ‘mobile’ and ‘immobile’ portions. A profit-shifting response will only be modelled for the mobile portion.

evidence.claim: In the UK and several other countries, policy costings rarely quantify macroeconomic effects beyond directly affected groups.
evidence.quote: It is important to note that, in most instances, these effects will be relatively small relative to the direct impact of a measure and may not be worth quantifying. In the UK, as well as Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States, it is very rare for the policy costing process to go further than considering behavioural effects for directly affected groups. However, in some cases, the effects may be more material and important to consider.

evidence.claim: The standard UK approach is to incorporate second-round macroeconomic effects as an ex post adjustment to an overall reform package rather than to specific policies, unless an individual policy has a particularly large macroeconomic effect.
evidence.quote: When costing the impact of a package of policies, one must also use judgement to determine whether to incorporate such second-round effects in the costings of specific policies or as an ex post adjustment to the overall package of reforms. In the UK, the typical approach is to do the latter unless any one individual policy is expected to have a particularly large effect on the macroeconomy.

evidence.claim: Companies may exhibit anticipatory profit-shifting responses prior to a reform, reducing the prior tax base and temporarily raising it following implementation.
evidence.quote: In reality, however, there may be some anticipatory responses as companies begin the process of profit-shifting in the period leading up to the reform. Companies may also shift their profits over time to take advantage of the new tax rate. This could decrease the size of the tax base in the year before the reform, and temporarily boost the size of the tax base after the reform has been introduced.

interpretations.statement: Interpretation: Raising the corporation tax main rate will mechanically increase the fiscal cost of existing corporate tax reliefs and capital allowances, partially offsetting the gross revenue yield from the higher statutory rate.

Interpretation: Standard UK policy costings for a corporation tax rate increase capture short- to medium-term behavioural erosion via international profit shifting and incorporation choices, but may overstate long-run net revenue gains if they omit direct effects on domestic business investment and treats macroeconomic feedback only as an ex post package adjustment.

Interpretation: While a higher statutory corporation tax rate increases the tax burden on equity-financed investment and increases subsidies for marginal debt-financed investment when combined with generous capital allowances, broader financial conditions—such as a 1 percentage point shift in market interest rates—can outweigh the cost-of-capital impact of statutory tax rate changes.

confounders.name: Macroeconomic and sectoral profit fluctuations
confounders.description: Revisions to nominal profits, nominal earnings, equity prices, and resilient performance in higher tax-paying sectors substantially alter onshore corporation tax receipts independently of statutory rate changes (for instance, higher nominal profits forecasts increased pre-measures receipts by £10 billion in 2030-31).

confounders.name: Concurrent capital allowance and tax relief regimes
confounders.description: Changes in investment allowances (such as the end of the super-deduction, the £1.3 billion AIA change, or full expensing peaking at £11 billion a year) and intellectual property reliefs (like the Patent Box) interact with the statutory rate and alter the net tax base and relief costs over time.

confounders.name: Multinational profit shifting and intertemporal anticipation
confounders.description: Firms can shift mobile profits across borders via transfer pricing and thin capitalization in response to statutory rate differentials, and may shift profits across time in anticipation of a pre-announced rate change, distorting the observed tax base immediately before and after implementation.

confounders.name: Income shifting and tax-motivated incorporation
confounders.description: Changes in the gap between personal and corporate tax rates induce behavioural responses in tax-motivated incorporation and the share of total income taken as corporate profit versus personal income.

confounders.name: Market interest rates
confounders.description: Fluctuations in market interest rates alter firms' cost of capital—where even a 1 percentage point rise in interest rates increases the cost of capital by more than raising the corporation tax rate from 19% to 25%—confounding empirical observations of how rate changes affect investment.

parameter_evidence.note: Evidence confirms that HMRC/OBR costings and academic studies estimate the elasticity of corporate taxable income (decomposed into total income, incorporation/personal-corporate shifting, and mobile profit-shifting elasticities), and notes a 29 percent marginal deadweight cost at the £10,000 kink [E3, E4, E5, E6, E32, E34], but does not provide the specific numerical elasticity parameter values.

Evidence indicates that companies may exhibit anticipatory profit-shifting responses prior to a reform and shift profits over time, affecting the tax base before and immediately after implementation [E37], but no numerical first-year fraction is stated.
